Do you guarantee that I’ll get a job?

About me

Hi, I'm Alisa

HR specialist and career consultant in Norway. I help people from all over the world understand how hiring here really works

My path

Before Norway

I was a lawyer at a large international pharmaceutical company. Long days, a lot of responsibility and two small kids at home

Starting again

Ten years ago we moved to Norway with our family. New language, new system, new rules. I knew one thing: I had to learn Norwegian - and I reached B2 in 13 months

Inside the system

My first job here was as a veileder at Nav, helping people find their way in the Norwegian welfare system. Then I became a career consultant at a private company, helping Nav’s clients find jobs. After that I worked in HR, and later again as a career consultant. I’ve also worked at Nav as a saksbehandler, handling sick-pay cases. Altogether I’ve run more than 370 interviews and seen the job market from both sides of the table

Today

I help people find their way into the Norwegian job market - calmly, honestly and step by step. Through my blog, my YouTube channel, the CV Guide and 1:1 workshops

Life outside work

Two hockey-playing sons, long road trips to tournaments, runs in the forest, autumn hikes in the mountains and our dog Loke, who's always by my side

Life in Norway

Moments from my life

Runs on the rocks by the sea, golf on sunny days, coffee by the ice rink during my sons’ hockey games - this is the Norway I want to help you build your life in

Job search

Call before you apply: the job hack most people skip

Most candidates click “apply” and wait. A 3-minute phone call can make the recruiter remember you before they even open your CV

In Norway, people don’t hire only on hard skills. They need to feel something personally about you. Most Norwegian job ads list a contact person with a phone number - that’s not decoration, it’s an invitation

Step 1. Introduce yourself

“Hi, my name is ___. I saw your position as ___, and it fits my experience well. I’m living in ___ and planning to move to Norway”
🇳🇴 In Norwegian: «Hei, jeg heter ___. Jeg så stillingen som ___, og jeg tror den passer godt til min erfaring. Jeg bor i ___ og planlegger å flytte til Norge»

Already in Norway? Simply skip the moving part and say where you live now

Step 2. Ask real questions about the job

Questions that work
?“Do you accept candidates from abroad?” - «Tar dere imot søkere fra utlandet?»
?“Is it worth applying?” - «Er det verdt å søke?»
?“What’s most important for you in this role?” - «Hva er viktigst for dere i denne stillingen?»
?“How is the work organised?” - «Hvordan er arbeidet organisert?»

Step 3. Mention the call in your application

“Thank you for our conversation on the phone. It made me even more motivated to apply”
🇳🇴 In Norwegian: «Takk for en hyggelig samtale på telefon. Den gjorde meg enda mer motivert til å søke»

Now you’re not just another CV - you’re the person they talked to

Scared to call?

Keep it short: 3-5 minutes is enough. Write down three sentences before you call. Recruiters talk to international candidates all the time

Interview

5 questions you’ll hear at every Norwegian job interview

The questions are not hard. The way Norwegian employers want you to answer them is different

The rule behind every answer
1Don’t start from who you are
2Start from who they’re looking for
3Then find that person in your own experience

1. “Tell me about yourself”

Short and clear: who you are, your experience and why you’re looking now. Add one active hobby - hiking, skiing, long walks. It says “full of energy” without saying it

2. “Describe yourself in a few words”

Use the words from their job ad - systematic, analytical, service-oriented, positive - and back each one up with one real example

3. “Tell me about a conflict at work”

The safest example is unclear responsibility: nobody knew who owned a task, you noticed it, talked it through and split the tasks clearly. No names, no villains

4. “What kind of colleagues are hard to work with?”

Describe a type, never a real person: “I find it harder with people who only see problems”

5. “How do you feel about automation and new systems?”

Be positive: technology takes the repetitive work, people still check and decide. Then add a real story of how you learned a new system

Bonus: salary

What you earned before is your private information. Ask about their range first. If they insist, give a range slightly above your target and add “rundt” - around

Practise your answers before the real interview

We take the real questions for your role and turn your experience into answers that sound like you - not like ChatGPT

Job search

You applied. Silence. Now what?

Silence after applying is one of the hardest parts of job hunting in Norway. But it doesn’t always mean no

Many Norwegian companies don’t even start reading applications before the deadline. And when they do, the process takes time. Ting tar tid - things take time

What to do while you wait
1Check the deadline (søknadsfrist). Give them 1-2 weeks after it
2Call the contact person - don’t just email
3Ask how many people applied and who they chose to interview
4Keep applying - finding a job here takes months for everyone

Got a no? Call and ask why

“I really liked this position. Could you tell me why you chose another candidate? What made them stronger?”
🇳🇴 In Norwegian: «Jeg likte stillingen veldig godt. Kan du fortelle hvorfor dere valgte en annen kandidat? Hva gjorde den kandidaten sterkere?»

Hiring managers post jobs again. They remember the people who called - and in a lot of situations they will be honest with you. Every answer makes your next application stronger

Job market

Jobs Norway needs most right now

Norwegian companies are short of about 34,000 workers. But the shortage is not where most people think

These numbers come from NAV’s company survey Bedriftsundersøkelsen 2026 - more than 13,000 Norwegian companies. Almost 1 in 5 tried to hire and couldn’t find the right person

Biggest shortages
1Health and care - 9,200 people (health care assistants, nurses)
2Industry - 5,750 people (industrial mechanics, energy fitters, welders)
3Building and construction - 4,750 people (carpenters, electricians)
Where the need is biggest
📍Vestland - 6,300
📍Rogaland - 3,750
📍Nordland - 2,950

The catch

A shortage doesn’t mean anyone gets hired. Health jobs need Norwegian authorisation and usually a good level of Norwegian. Trades need recognised qualifications. Employers want the right person, not just any person

Source: Nav, Bedriftsundersøkelsen 2026

Networking

How people really get jobs in Norway

When Randstad asked people in Norway how they got their last job, most said: through someone they knew

Norway is a small job market. When a manager needs someone new, one of the first questions is often “does anyone know someone who could do this?” You don’t need a big network from day one. You need to become visible

Three ways to become visible
1Call the contact person before you apply
2Connect with people in your field on LinkedIn - and actually write to them
3Tell everyone you’re looking: neighbours, former colleagues, other parents at training. Still abroad? Start with Norwegians in your field on LinkedIn and people from your country who already live here

Write personal messages

General messages are not interesting to anyone. Be specific:

“I see you’re working with ___ in Norway. Could we have five minutes to talk? I’d love a few tips on how to get started in this field”
🇳🇴 In Norwegian: «Jeg ser at du jobber med ___ i Norge. Har du fem minutter til en prat? Jeg vil gjerne høre noen tips om hvordan man kommer inn i bransjen»

Online applications still matter. They’re just one channel out of several

Work culture

Things that feel rude in a Norwegian office (but aren’t)

Short emails, everyone leaving at 4 pm, nobody saying “great job”. Most of it isn’t rude at all

What it really means
✓Short emails with no “Dear” - respect for your time
✓Everyone leaves at 4 pm - work time is work time, family time matters too
✓You call your boss by first name - the hierarchy is flat and your opinion is expected
✓Silence in meetings - people think before they speak
✓Quiet feedback - a short “bra jobba” is a real compliment
✓No to after-work - the real connection happens at lunch

Norwegian work culture is built on trust, a flat hierarchy and respect for people’s time. Once you understand the rules, a lot of “rude” things start to feel… actually pretty nice

Work permit

Why it took my client 1.5 years to move to Norway

He had a job offer from a big factory. Everything looked simple. It took 18 months - because of one paragraph in his job offer

📄
The offer
A job offer as a refrigeration mechanic at a big crab processing factory. It just said “refrigeration mechanic - repair and maintenance of refrigerator facility”. Nothing about what the work actually involved
⏳
Waiting
He applied to UDI. Four months of processing, plus a month of summer delays because almost the whole office was on vacation
❌
Rejection
UDI said the employer hadn’t proven that the job actually required a qualified mechanic. To everyone else it was obvious - a massive industrial refrigeration facility needs real certification. But UDI wanted proof
✍️
Appeal
We spent weeks sending extra documents to explain what should have been obvious
✅
Approved
Two months later - approval. After the visa, tickets and all the delays he finally arrived. 1.5 years in total

Why did this happen?

Because the job offer wasn’t detailed enough for UDI. They don’t guess - they read exactly what is written

What a strong job offer includes
✓Not just the job title - what you’ll actually do every day
✓Why the job requires your exact education and qualifications
✓Salary and working hours that meet Norwegian standards
✓A clear start date and the type of contract
Your job offer matters more than you think. Read it before you send anything to UDI - or let someone who knows the system read it with you
